blocks.text: Χειροδροπὰ δ' ἵνα φῶτες ἄνευ δρεπάνοιο λέγονται Ὄσπρια, χεδροπά τ' ἄλλα, μεσοχλόου ἐντὸς ἀρούρης· [Cheirodropa d' hina phōtes aneu drepanoio legontai / Ospria, chedropa t' alla, mesochlou entos arourēs]

Where men gather by hand, without a sickle, pulses and other things of that kind, in the half-green field. Once these points are noted, it will at once be clear what Josephus means when he says that dove's dung served the Samaritans in place of salt. Theophrastus (De causis plantarum, book 4, chapter 9), inquiring into the reasons why the chickpea ripens sooner than other pulses, gives this one among others: Ἡ ἅλμη πρὸς τὴν τελείωσιν συμβάλλεται [Hē halmē pros tēn teleiōsin symballetai], The saltiness of the chickpea contributes to that quick ripening. And in book 5, chapter 11: Ὁ ἐρέβινθος ἀπόλλυται σφακελίας, ὅταν ἀνθοῦσιν ὕδωρ ἐπιγινόμενον ἐπικλύσῃ τὴν ἄλμην· τὸ γὰρ ἔφαλμα οἷον σφακελίζειν ἐστί [Ho erebinthos apollytai sphakelias, hotan anthousin hydōr epiginomenon epiklysē tēn halmēn; to gar ephalma hoion sphakelizein esti]. The chickpea perishes of blight when rain washes off its saltiness while it is in flower: for the loss of its saltiness is to it a kind of blight. Cato too says of the chickpea, in De re rustica, chapter 37: If you sow chickpea in crumbly soil, since it is pulled up, it is salty and harmful. And Columella, book 2, chapter 14, says that Tremellius states that the soil is harmed most [II, 589] by the poison of chickpea and flax: the one because it is of a salty nature, the other because it is of a hot nature. And Pliny, book 18, chapter 12: It is the nature of the chickpea to grow with saltiness; therefore it burns the soil. And in book 17: A defect common to all crops is blight, the chickpea's too, when the rain, washing off its saltiness, makes it sweeter. Galen, in book 6 of De simplic., calls this bitterness, when he says of chickpeas: Μετέχουσι δέ τι καὶ τῆς πικρότητος [Metechousi de ti kai tēs pikrotētos]; They also have something of bitterness. And of the wild chickpea: Δριμύτερός τ᾽ ἐστι, καὶ πικρότερος [Drimyteros t' esti, kai pikroteros], It is sharper and more bitter. But he put bitter for salty, as when the Poet says of the sea,

Accordingly, as we have noted, the Arabs extract from a certain kind of chickpea that very famous salt which is therefore called sal alkali, that is, salt of burnt chickpea. So, on the passage with which we are dealing, when the older Hebrews had remarked that it was dove's dung, from which salt is extracted, this was misunderstood by Josephus, who wrote that at Samaria dove's dung was used ἀντὶ ἁλῶν [anti halōn], in place of salt. Hence Theodoret on 4 Kings, Question 21: Ἡ τῆς πολιορκίας ἀνάγκη, καὶ τοῦ λίμου τὸ μέγεθος ἠνάγκασεν αὐτοὺς ἀντὶ ἁλῶν κεχρῆσθαι τῷ κόπρῳ [Hē tēs poliorkias anankē, kai tou limou to megethos ēnankasen autous anti halōn kechrēsthai tō koprō]. The necessity of the siege and the severity of the famine compelled them to use dung in place of salt ^{(9)}.
